If you've found yourself sweeping down cobwebs in the same corner of your garage for the third time this month, you're not imagining it — spiders are creatures of habit, and once they find a reliable food and shelter source, they keep coming back (and so do their relatives). Understanding why spiders choose your home in the first place is the key to actually keeping them out, rather than just knocking down webs on repeat.

## Why Spiders Move Indoors in the First Place

Spiders aren't trying to bother you. They're hunting. Every spider in your home is there because something drew it in — usually insects, moisture, or an easy entry point. If you've got spiders, you almost certainly have one of these three conditions somewhere nearby.

**They follow their food supply.** Spiders eat other bugs — flies, moths, ants, roaches, even other spiders. A home with a spider problem usually has an underlying insect problem feeding them. If you've noticed more gnats near windows or ants along the baseboards, the spiders showed up because the buffet did.

**They love dark, undisturbed spaces.** Basements, crawl spaces, garage corners, and the gap behind stored boxes are prime real estate. Spiders prefer places that don't get swept or vacuumed often, so clutter is basically a welcome mat.

**They need moisture.** Many common house spiders, especially cellar spiders and wolf spiders, are drawn to damp areas — think laundry rooms, under sinks, or crawl spaces with poor drainage.

## Why This Matters More Here in Kansas

Our Kansas homes see a wider temperature swing than most regions, and that swing is exactly what pushes spiders indoors twice a year instead of once. In late summer and early fall, as outdoor temps start dropping at night but days are still warm, spiders migrate toward structures looking for stable shelter before winter. Then in early spring, as the ground thaws and insect activity picks back up, a second wave moves in chasing the bugs that are waking up first.

Older housing stock throughout our service area compounds the problem. Homes built before the 1980s often have gaps around foundation sills, older weatherstripping, and window frames that have shifted slightly over decades — all easy entry points for a spider that's an eighth of an inch thick and can flatten itself through a gap you'd never notice. Combine that with the humid summers typical of our region, which keep basements and crawl spaces consistently damp, and you've got conditions that are genuinely more favorable to spider activity than a lot of other parts of the country.

## The Species You're Actually Dealing With

Most spiders found in and around area homes fall into a handful of common categories: cellar spiders (the long-legged ones in basement corners), wolf spiders (larger, fast-moving, often mistaken for something more dangerous), common house spiders, and occasionally cobweb spiders near outdoor lighting where insects congregate. The good news is the vast majority of what people find indoors is harmless — a nuisance, not a danger. For a closer look at identification and when a sighting is actually something to worry about, our [pest control spiders](/pest-control-spiders/) page breaks down what's commonly seen in this area and how to tell them apart.

## What Actually Works (And What Doesn't)

**Killing the ones you see does nothing long-term.** If you're only reacting to spiders you spot, you're treating a symptom. More are already behind the walls, in the attic, or under the porch, and new ones will keep arriving as long as the conditions that attracted them stay the same.

**Reduce the food source first.** This is the step most homeowners skip. If you're dealing with ants, roaches, or seasonal invaders like stink bugs or boxelder bugs, addressing those populations removes the reason spiders are showing up at all. Our [pest control ants](/pest-control-ants/) and [pest control roaches](/pest-control-roaches/) pages cover the most common culprits we see feeding spider populations in homes throughout the area.

**Seal entry points.** Caulk gaps around foundation sills, window frames, and utility penetrations (where pipes and wires enter the home). Weatherstripping worn doors. This single step eliminates a huge percentage of new spider entries, especially during the fall and spring migration windows.

**Manage moisture.** Run a dehumidifier in persistently damp basements or crawl spaces. Fix any slow leaks under sinks. Make sure gutters are directing water away from the foundation rather than pooling against it.

**Clear clutter in storage areas.** Garages, attics, and basements with stacked boxes directly on the floor give spiders exactly the undisturbed space they want. Elevating stored items and leaving a few inches of clearance from walls makes those areas far less appealing.

**Treat the perimeter, not just the interior.** A perimeter barrier treatment around the foundation, applied by a licensed technician, interrupts spiders before they ever reach your door, rather than waiting to deal with them once they're already inside.

## When to Call a Professional

A few spiders in the garage once in a while is normal. It's time to bring in a professional when you're seeing spiders consistently across multiple rooms, finding egg sacs indoors, noticing a spike in web activity in a short window, or dealing with a species you can't confidently identify. A trained technician can also spot the entry points and moisture issues a homeowner might miss, and treat both the insects spiders are feeding on and the spiders themselves in one visit.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Why do I keep finding spiders in the same spot even after I clean it?**
If a corner, closet, or basement area keeps producing spiders, there's an ongoing attractant nearby — usually a food source (other insects) or a moisture issue. Cleaning removes the webs but not the reason spiders chose that spot.

**Are the spiders I'm finding dangerous?**
The large majority of spiders found inside homes in our area are harmless, including wolf spiders despite their intimidating size. Venomous species exist but are far less commonly encountered indoors than people assume.

**Does spraying for spiders actually work, or do I need something else?**
Spray treatments help, but they're most effective as part of a broader approach that also addresses entry points and the insect food source. Spray alone without sealing gaps just means new spiders replace the ones you treated.

**How often should a home be treated for spiders?**
Most homes in our region benefit from treatment aligned with the two seasonal migration windows — early fall and early spring — plus spot treatment if activity spikes in between.

**Can spiders come back even after a professional treatment?**
Some re-entry is possible, especially if new gaps develop or a nearby insect population rebounds. That's why ongoing service plans typically include periodic re-treatment rather than a single visit.

**Do ultrasonic pest repellers actually keep spiders away?**
There's no reliable evidence that ultrasonic devices meaningfully reduce spider activity. Sealing entry points and addressing food/moisture sources has a far more consistent track record.

Spiders showing up isn't bad luck — it's a response to conditions your home is currently offering. Fix the conditions, and the spiders stop showing up.
